title: Find Pattern in Infinite Stream I
statement:
This is an interactive problem. An endless stream of bits (each `0` or `1`) has its positions numbered from `0`. You cannot see it all at once: the object `infiniteStream` has a single method, `infiniteStream.next()`, which returns the next bit each time it is called (position `0` on the first call, then position `1`, and so on). You are also given a binary array `pattern`.

Return the smallest index `i` such that the bits at positions `i` through `i + pattern.length - 1` of the stream are exactly `pattern`. The pattern is guaranteed to start somewhere within the first 10^5 bits.

Your function is `findPattern(infiniteStream, pattern)`. Each case is written as `[stream, pattern]`, where `stream` is a block of bits that repeats forever to form the endless stream (so `[1, 0, 1]` stands for `1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, ...`). The judge builds `infiniteStream` from it; your function never sees `stream` itself, and a solution that calls `next` more than 100,100 times in one case is stopped.
constraints: The pattern starts within the first 10^5 bits of the stream
In a case, 1 <= stream.length <= 2000 (the block that repeats forever)
api: findPattern(infiniteStream: InfiniteStream, pattern: number[]): number, with interface InfiniteStream { next(): number }
notes:
## Intuition

The stream can only be read forward, one bit at a time, so we want to decide after each bit whether the pattern has just been completed. The brute force keeps every bit read and, after each one, compares the last `m` bits with `pattern`: O(m) work per bit. Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP) does better: it tracks how many leading bits of the pattern the stream currently ends with, and on a mismatch it falls back to the longest shorter prefix that still fits, using a table built from the pattern alone. No bit is ever re-read.

## Approach

1. Build `lps`: `lps[i]` is the length of the longest proper prefix of `pattern[0..i]` that is also a suffix of it. Walk `i` from 1 and keep `len`, falling back through `lps` while the next bit disagrees.
2. Read bits with `next()`, counting their positions in `index`. Keep `matched`, the number of pattern bits the stream currently ends with.
3. While `bit` does not continue the match, fall back with `matched = lps[matched - 1]`.
4. If `bit` equals `pattern[matched]`, extend the match.
5. When `matched` reaches `m`, the pattern ends at `index`, so return `index - m + 1`.

## Example 1, step by step

`pattern = [0, 1]` gives `lps = [0, 0]`. The stream starts `1, 1, 1, 0, 1`. At indexes 0 to 2 the bit is 1, which is not `pattern[0]`, so `matched` stays 0. At index 3 the bit 0 matches, `matched = 1`. At index 4 the bit 1 equals `pattern[1]`, `matched = 2 = m`, so the answer is `4 - 2 + 1 = 3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m + s), where s is the number of bits read (the answer plus m): each bit raises `matched` at most once, and every fallback lowers it.
- Space: O(m) for `lps`; the stream itself is never stored.

## Pitfalls

- Do not reset `matched` to 0 on a mismatch: in `1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1` with pattern `[1, 0, 1, 1]`, the second `1, 0, 1` overlaps the first and leads to the match at index 2.
- The stream cannot be rewound, so a restart-from-the-next-position search must keep the bits it has read.
- Return the starting index, not the index of the last matched bit.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `m` | length of `pattern` |
| `lps` | longest proper prefix that is also a suffix, for each pattern prefix |
| `len` | current prefix length while building `lps` |
| `index` | position of the bit just read |
| `bit` | the bit just read from the stream |
| `matched` | how many leading pattern bits the stream currently ends with |

narration.2: Remember the pattern length; a match is complete when this many bits line up.
narration.3: lps[i] will hold the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also its suffix.
narration.5: Build the table from the second pattern bit onward.
narration.6: The next bit breaks the current prefix, so fall back to a shorter one.
narration.7: Jump to the longest shorter prefix that still fits.
narration.10: ...so the matching prefix grows by one.
narration.12: Store the prefix length for pattern[0..i].
narration.14: No pattern bits are matched before reading the stream.
narration.15: Read the stream forever; index is the position of the bit just read.
narration.16: Read one bit; the stream cannot be rewound.
narration.17: This bit cannot continue the current match, so fall back.
narration.18: Keep the longest shorter prefix that the stream still ends with.
narration.21: ...so one more pattern bit is matched.
narration.23: All m bits match, ending at index.
